rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A 10-minute gradient and intermediate temperature provide a useful baseline for optimizing resolution and run time.

Change temperature while holding the gradient fixed to probe selectivity in the crowded central cluster. The current elution window leaves ample room to improve the critical separation without incurring a time penalty.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity limit with the same gradient, since heating improved one crowded region but created a different critical pair. The initial run's short elution window provides room for the increased retention expected on cooling.

Use a temperature between the two strongest runs to balance the competing central separations, and a shallower gradient to increase their resolution. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes given the retention margin in those runs.

Raise temperature one step from injection 4 to improve the remaining central critical pair. The shallower gradient may preserve enough separation in the earlier cluster that was limiting at 55 C with the 10-minute gradient.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This tests whether the earlier critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5 between the successful 14-minute and deficient 10-minute gradients.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether altered early retention restores the limiting separation with the shorter gradient. Keep injection 5 as the maximum-score fallback while exploring a faster fully resolved method.

Test a faster, hotter gradient for an alternative selectivity window beyond the apparent crossing of the earlier critical pair. This exploratory run may recover separation after an elution-order reversal, while injections 5 and 7 remain maximum-score fallbacks.

Shorten the hot gradient one step to test whether the reversed critical pair separates further as slope increases. Monitor the neighboring gap, which may become limiting as the central cluster compresses.

Test starting-composition selectivity at the faster, hotter setting, since shortening alone compressed a neighboring separation. Raising phi0 may widen the reversed critical pair while reducing retention; check that the early peaks remain resolved.

Probe an intermediate cool-temperature selectivity window, since the faster 60 C methods trade one unresolved pair for another. This fills the gap between the 25 C and 40 C scouts while retaining a comfortably short elution window.

Refine the promising 55 C region by slightly reducing gradient slope relative to injection 6. This tests whether a modest increase in separation can restore full resolution with an elution time shorter than injection 7.

Shorten the fully resolved low-starting-organic method while reducing the endpoint to limit the increase in gradient slope. This probes the faster boundary near injection 7, with particular attention to its two marginal central separations.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 12 to lift its nearly resolved critical pair above R = 1.5. This should provide a second balanced, fully resolved method with a last peak still comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether a shallower gradient resolves the central bottleneck at 40 C, providing an alternative fully resolved selectivity window. Comparing directly with injection 1 isolates the slope effect while the last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from injection 5 to shorten retention while retaining its successful temperature and gradient duration. This tests whether the slightly shallower slope offsets the adverse starting-composition effect on the earlier critical separation.

Preserve injection 7's successful gradient slope and starting composition while ending the programmed ramp two minutes earlier. All peaks previously eluted before this new endpoint, so this should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test whether raising the starting organic fraction improves the remaining critical separation in injection 15 while shortening retention. This explores a cooler alternative without lengthening that run toward the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Use a gradient slope between injections 12 and 14 to target full resolution with less retention than injection 14. The 0.75 endpoint remains above the composition at which the last peak eluted in those runs, limiting truncation risk.

Increase gradient duration one step from injection 16 to recover its earlier critical separation while retaining the improved margin in the later pair. This tests a potentially more balanced maximum-score method, with the last peak expected below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 20's gradient to bring its R = 1.41 pair above the resolution threshold while preserving the other central pair's margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially yielding a maximum-score method with greater minimum resolution.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving the starting composition and slope of the fastest fully resolved method. Its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this ramp ends at the outlet, so the same maximum CRF is expected with a lower endpoint.

Raise temperature one grid step from injection 22 to test whether its fully resolved method can elute faster. Monitor the earlier central pair for a selectivity loss; retain the 55 C method if resolution falls below 1.5.

Return to the successful 55 C temperature and increase the endpoint one step to test the faster slope boundary of injection 22. If the earlier critical pair falls below R = 1.5, retain injection 22 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Preserve injection 22's successful slope through the critical cluster, then test an earlier transition to the final hold. This may retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed ramp, although the last peak may elute later; injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved choice.
